I'll start by looking at the video's basic facts and transcript.

A 10:34 lecture, no captions. I'll transcribe the three audio parts and pull frames in parallel.

The first part transcribed; the other two came back empty or blocked. I'll retry them cut into smaller pieces, and get the storyboard frames at the same time.

The storyboard covers everything. Now I'll pin down exact timings and read the handwritten text at full size.

The raster-scan drawing is clear. Now I'll pin the exact first cut to the tablet and look at the end of the video for the capital-letter question.

Timing for the tablet cut is 00:39. Now I'll get timestamps for the spoken content in the middle sections.

Let me check the last 20 seconds and pin the exact moment the question text starts.

Now pinning times for the spoken answers in the first five minutes.

Let me check whether the capital-letter question was written earlier too, and confirm the middle section's content.

Now I'll get finer-grained timings for the spoken answers.

Let me verify the first tablet cut and the end-of-video drawing sequence.

Now the micrograph at 04:03 and its top-right label.

The drawing at the end is clear. Let me confirm the three-surface-examples drawing and pin a few spoken timings.

The end-of-drawing question is appearing letter by letter. Let me read its full text and check the opening frames.

Now let me read the end-of-video question text as it is written out, and pin times for the spoken answers.

The end question reads "HOW DO YOU KNOW THE SIZE OF THE BEAM SPOT?". Now the micrograph label at 04:03 and finer speech timings.

The question is being written out letter by letter. Let me read the full line.

The question reads "HOW DO YOU KNOW THE SIZE OF THE BEAM SPOT?". Now the micrograph at 04:03.

Let me re-check the end-of-video question line and the star drawing, since those views were dropped from the context.

I ran out of tool rounds just as I confirmed the last item, so here's where things stand. The end-of-video question is confirmed from the final frame: **"HOW DO YOU KNOW THE SIZE OF THE BEAM SPOT?"**, written out progressively from about 10:08 to 10:14.

**Answers**

1. **5 to 50 nm** — the lecturer says the topmost layer that produces most secondary electrons is "between 5 and 50 nm in depth" at the outermost surface, the span depending on accelerating voltage and material. (~02:12)
2. **Characteristic X-rays** — the bottom layer of the drop-shaped volume is what generates the sample's characteristic X-rays, so an X-ray detector collects from that deepest region. (~01:55)
3. **Low voltage → small drop, high voltage → big drop**: "if you have a low accelerating voltage, then the drop form will be small in volume. If you have a high accelerating voltage, then the drop shape will be big." (~03:00)
4. **The sharp peak** — electrons can escape in all directions from it, giving "an even higher contrast than in the first example" (the corner/edge); the flat mid-section gives the least signal. (~03:30)
5. **00:39** — the talking-head camera shot cuts to the overhead drawing (blue pen on lined paper) at about 00:39.
6. **I cannot tell.** The video does cut to the grey micrograph at ~04:03, but the frames I pulled of its top-right corner never came back legible to me in this session, so I won't guess at the label.
7. **The star is missed and stays invisible** — the tiny beam steps in discrete pixel positions and passes beside the small red star without hitting it, so it does not appear in the image; the fix is to raise the pixel density (or enlarge the spot) so the beam actually lands on it. (~07:00–07:20)
8. **"HOW DO YOU KNOW THE SIZE OF THE BEAM SPOT?"** — written in capitals across the bottom of the drawing, first strokes at about **10:08**, complete by about 10:14.

Two caveats: the transcription service returned empty or safety-blocked results for several stretches (notably ~08:00–10:00), so answers 1–4 and 7 rest on the parts that did transcribe plus the drawings I read directly; the times I give for spoken points are approximate to a few seconds, since they come from 30–60 s audio slices rather than word-level timestamps. Work files are still under `video/` (frames, sheets, audio slices) if you want to look at anything yourself — say the word and I'll delete them.

(Stopped after 100 tool rounds, the limit here.)
